summary:
NISAR, the radar satellite NASA and ISRO launched in 2025, images nearly all of Earth's land every 12 days, day or night and through clouds. Its data is public, but hard to read. SARstellar teaches you to read it, using only real NISAR data.

NISAR measures every echo two ways. HH is strongest when the pulse bounces off water and tree trunks, or streets and walls. HV comes from pulses scattered inside leaves and branches. Each kind of change moves these two numbers differently. In Punjab, wheat raised HV by 3.3 dB over the winter, and rice planted in standing water raised HH by 6.9 dB in the same fields. Floodwater under a Texas forest raised HH while HV stayed flat. Forest clearing in the Amazon cut HV by about 7.5 dB.

We trained a model on 170 US sites and tested it on 72 sites in 12 states it had never seen. It found 54% of forest loss while flagging 1.7% of the land, and HV alone found forest loss about 6 times better than HH alone. You can also draw a box anywhere in the US and compare what NISAR and Sentinel-1 detected there.
details:
What it does

SARstellar is a guided website about what NISAR's radar sees on Earth's surface. Every image and chart on it comes from real NISAR passes. https://github.com/saa938/sarstellar

It starts with how the radar listens. NISAR sends 24 cm microwave pulses and records each echo in two polarizations. HH is the part that comes back with the same orientation it was sent, and it is strongest when the pulse bounces between water and a tree trunk, or a street and a wall. HV is the part that comes back rotated after bouncing around inside leaves and branches, so it tracks vegetation. Plot every hectare by these two values and water, bare soil, crops, forest and cities each land in their own part of the chart.

Then it walks through five real changes, each with before and after radar images, a chart of the hectares moving between passes, and one measured number. In Punjab, India, the median HV of 70,752 cultivated hectares rose 3.3 dB from November to February as wheat grew. In the same fields, the median HH rose 6.9 dB from July to September, when rice stood in flooded paddies. In Village Creek, Texas, on the pass during Tropical Storm Edouard, 3,572 forested hectares rose at least 3 dB in HH while HV held steady: floodwater under the trees. Twelve days later it had drained. In Rondônia, Brazil, cleared forest lost about 7.5 dB of HV between June and October. On the Greenland ice sheet, HH rose 4 to 5 dB across the melt zone at the peak of summer and settled by October.

Places plays every NISAR pass over nine places with the chart moving in sync. Analyze lets you draw a box up to 20 km across anywhere in the US, see where NISAR (L-band) and Sentinel-1 (C-band) detected change hectare by hectare, and click a change to see what changed and when. Benchmark scores the two radars on US reference sites. Method explains the data, the model, every number and the limits.

Does it work?

We trained a gradient-boosted model on the change in HH and HV between two NISAR passes. The labels come from independent sources: NASA OPERA DIST-ALERT-HLS for forest loss, NIFC wildfire perimeters, OPERA DSWx for water, and the USDA Cropland Data Layer. Training used 170 US sites. Testing used 72 sites in 12 states the model never saw. That is 2.46 million reference hectares in total.

On the unseen states it found 54% of forest loss while flagging 1.7% of the land. Picking that much land at random would find about 2%. When it says a field is growing a crop, it is right 63% of the time, against 10% by chance. Retraining with one polarization at a time answers the challenge's question about polarizations: HV alone finds forest loss about 6 times better than HH alone, because the canopy echo is what disappears. Trained only on US sites, it still found 54% of the forest loss that NASA's optical alerts recorded in Rondônia. On 37 forest-loss sites, NISAR's alerts were right 7.8 times more often than Sentinel-1's at the same detection rate.

Some things don't work yet, and the site says so. Open-water floods could not be told apart from two passes at our flood reference sites. Grass fires barely register at L-band. Floods under trees and ice changes have no labeled test set, so we show them as measured physics, not tested results. NISAR's 2026 data are provisional releases.

Who it helps

NISAR's data only became public in 2026, and almost nobody outside radar science can read it yet. SARstellar is for students, teachers, resource managers and anyone curious. It shows with real measurements what L-band radar adds. The same signals could support deforestation alerts in the tropics when clouds block optical satellites, flood maps under forest canopy, rice planting estimates for food security, crop calendars for any farming region, and tracking the melt season on ice sheets every 12 days.

How we built it

Python does the science. We search NASA's CMR for calibrated NISAR L2 GCOV products, group the passes into same-mode series for each orbit track, read only the parts of each 2 to 9 GB HDF5 file we need over HTTPS, and average them into 1-hectare blocks. The reads ran in parallel on Modal, one container per file, and we trained the model there with LightGBM. The website is React and TypeScript with canvas charts, and the analysis map uses MapLibre. It is hosted on Vercel. We rendered the demo video frame by frame in three.js from the same NISAR data and NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery. All of it is open source under Apache-2.0: https://github.com/saa938/sarstellar

What makes it creative

The challenge describes Earth's surface as a dance, and we took that literally. Each kind of change has its own movement through NISAR's two channels, and you watch the hectares move across the chart pass by pass. The same Punjab fields move twice a year, once in HV for wheat and once in HH for rice. The goal is that after a few minutes on the site, a visitor can look at a change in NISAR data and say what probably happened and why.

What we considered

Honesty came first. Every number on the site comes from our own pipeline, accuracy is measured on states the model never saw, and the limits sit next to the results. We used only calibrated NISAR products. We chose places where independent reference data exist and dropped places where the data did not clearly show a change, like an Indiana flood that had already drained before NISAR's next pass. We kept the language plain so a student and a radar scientist can both follow it.
